content: Individuals seeking testing or treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are at an increased risk of HIV infection, presenting an opportunity for HIV screening. Providing STI services to people living with HIV is essential for a comprehensive approach to sexual and reproductive health and rights. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations for STI screening and treatment, which include the following: 1. Management of Urethral Discharge in Men: This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. 2. Management of Vaginal Discharge in Women: WHO advises treatment for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and/or Trichomonas vaginalis during the same visit. This is also a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 3. Lower Abdominal Pain in Sexually Active Women: WHO suggests assessing for pelvic inflammatory disease and providing syndromic treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 4. Genital Ulcers (Including Anorectal Ulcers): WHO recommends treatment based on molecular assay results of the ulcer. In settings without molecular testing, syndromic treatment should be initiated on the same day. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 5. Anorectal Discharge in Individuals Reporting Receptive Anal Sex: Management should be based on molecular assay results. In the absence of molecular testing, syndromic treatment should be provided during the visit. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. The lack of affordable, reliable point-of-care tests for STIs (except for syphilis) in many regions means that treatment often relies on symptom-based diagnosis. Clear and consistent case definitions are critical for monitoring appropriate treatment in such cases. STI data can be collected from various HIV programs, including prevention services, testing clinics, and care facilities. Viral Hepatitis and HIV Co-Infection Hepatitis B (HBV) and Hepatitis C (HCV) infections contribute significantly to global disease burden, with over one million deaths annually due to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. In 2019, an estimated 296 million people were living with chronic HBV, and 58 million with HCV. The burden is concentrated in specific geographic regions and populations, including economically disadvantaged areas, displaced individuals, and people who inject drugs. Co-infection with HIV accelerates the progression of liver disease and increases mortality. Comprehensive, person-centered approaches are necessary in high-risk populations to integrate hepatitis screening into HIV prevention services. Cervical Cancer and HIV Women living with HIV have a six-fold higher risk of cervical cancer compared to HIV-negative women. This increased risk is due to higher susceptibility to HPV infection, slower regression of precancerous lesions, faster progression to cancer, and higher recurrence rates after treatment. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has improved life expectancy, but cervical cancer remains a significant concern, particularly in regions with high HIV prevalence. WHO recommends starting cervical cancer screening at age 25 for women living with HIV, using an HPV DNA detection approach with regular screening every 3–5 years. Strong referral systems between HIV and cervical cancer services are essential. Global Strategies and Data Integration The WHO Global Strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem by 2030 includes the following targets: 90% of girls fully vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by age 15. 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45. 90% of women with cervical disease treated appropriately. Data collection and monitoring are critical for achieving these goals. WHO emphasizes the need for disaggregated data by age, sex, and other characteristics to identify inequalities and track progress. Conclusion Comprehensive integration of STI, viral hepatitis, and cervical cancer services into HIV programs is essential for improving health outcomes. WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to support countries in scaling up access to modern, high-quality screening and treatment technologies, ultimately reducing morbidity and mortality associated with these conditions.
